headline: One Health: AMR transmission with Natacha Couto and Ed Feil
description: Natacha Couto and Ed Feil discuss One Health, AMR transmission, sampling bias and why resistance genes do not always mean resistant bacteria.
summary: Natacha Couto of the University of Oxford and Ed Feil of the University of Bath join the hosts to examine One Health, with antimicrobial resistance as a central example. They question diagrams that imply unrestricted movement between humans, animals and the environment, and discuss evidence from a large Klebsiella study. The conversation explains why sampling methods, ecological barriers and host context matter when interpreting transmission and disease risk.

people.name: Lee Katz
people.affiliation: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention; University of Georgia

sections.heading: One Health is broader than AMR
sections.body:
Ed introduces One Health as a framework that developed from One Medicine. For antimicrobial resistance (AMR), it means considering antibiotic use and resistance in healthcare, agriculture and environmental settings such as rivers and soils, rather than treating hospitals as isolated systems.

Natacha emphasises that One Health is not limited to AMR or even to bacterial disease: viruses, fungi and parasites also belong within it. Its wider purpose is to improve health across connected sectors and learn from their different perspectives. AMR is a particularly useful example because it connects so many of those settings.

sections.heading: What the One Health arrows leave out
sections.body:
The guests call the familiar diagram of people, animals, hospitals and environmental compartments connected by arrows a One Health “confusogram”. They accept that transmission can occur, but argue that arrows alone do not quantify its frequency or consequences. A spillover that infects one host without onward transmission is different from a strain establishing itself in a new population.

Ed argues that attractive figures can carry an unstated hypothesis: that movement is effectively unimpeded. Testing that assumption means investigating ecological barriers, host adaptation and local competition. It also means distinguishing movement of bacterial strains from movement of resistance genes and mobile elements, which adds another layer of complexity.

sections.heading: Sampling bias and the SPARK study
sections.body:
Ed explains that adding antibiotics to culture media improves the chance of detecting resistant bacteria, but does not necessarily reveal how common they are in the sampled setting. He contrasts this with SPARK, a study he says had just been accepted by Nature Microbiology.

SPARK sampled hospitals, communities, farms and environmental sites around Pavia in northern Italy over roughly 15 months. The region had a high hospital prevalence of KPC-producing Klebsiella. Without selecting for antibiotic resistance, the researchers sequenced approximately 3,500 genomes and found no carbapenem-non-susceptible Klebsiella pneumoniae outside hospitals, either genotypically or phenotypically.

This did not establish that such bacteria were absent. Ed suggests hospital-adapted clones may be outcompeted outside healthcare, while stressing that findings from northern Italy need not apply to settings with different antibiotic use or human–animal contact.

sections.heading: Resistance genes, expression and fitness costs
sections.body:
A host asks whether maintaining resistance must impose a substantial metabolic burden. Ed replies that experimental evidence varies: some resistance genes or plasmids carry fitness costs, while others show little apparent cost.

In a Bath river study, the guests describe bacteria carrying OXA-48 resistance plasmids without being phenotypically resistant. Selecting for resistance would have missed those plasmids. Natacha also discusses work in human patients where mutations could silence resistance-gene expression, and examples of plasmids expanding alongside particular bacterial clones. Their point is that gene carriage, expression, measured resistance and fitness cannot be treated as interchangeable observations.

sections.heading: Why pathogen and commensal are contextual labels
sections.body:
Natacha uses secondary bacterial infections in dogs with atopic dermatitis to explain how organisms present in healthy hosts can cause disease when the host–microbe balance changes. Ed agrees that context matters, while noting that some organisms are clearly more dangerous than others.

Their examples include Clostridioides difficile overgrowth and E. coli occupying different sites in the body. Disease potential can depend on the microbial community, anatomical location and relatively small genomic changes. Even a proposed virulence factor such as a flagellum is not inherently harmful: Ed points to free-swimming Vibrio splendidus as a counterexample. Virulence therefore cannot be read from a simple list of “bad” organisms or genes.

sections.heading: Where to look, and which questions to ask
sections.body:
The panel separates immediate infection control from understanding where resistance and virulence originate. Ed prioritises healthcare and community outbreaks for day-to-day control, particularly in high-resource settings. Broader questions require studying commensals and non-human systems, including plants, insects and wildlife. Natacha describes the unresolved resource choice between sequencing resistant pathogens and examining susceptible populations before problems expand.

Shared sequencing and analysis tools do not make the epidemiology interchangeable. Tick-borne transmission requires understanding reservoir hosts such as deer, pheasants and shrews; simple hospital contact models are insufficient. Host switches, COVID-19 and habitat changes illustrate further complications. Human-community studies also need social science: behaviour, risk perception, adherence to advice and antibiotic use can all affect transmission.

quotes.text: AMR has been described as a quintessential One Health problem because of this interconnectedness between all the different sort of settings that we have.
quotes.speaker: Ed Feil

quotes.text: I think the tools available are the same but the questions are very different.
quotes.speaker: Natacha Couto

faq.q: Is One Health only about antimicrobial resistance?
faq.a: No. Natacha explains that it also encompasses diseases involving viruses, fungi and parasites, and more broadly seeks to improve health across connected human, animal and environmental sectors.

faq.q: What is the problem with One Health transmission diagrams?
faq.a: Arrows show possible connections without measuring how often transmission occurs or whether it leads to onward spread. The guests argue that ecological and biological barriers must be tested rather than assuming unrestricted movement.

faq.q: What did the SPARK study find outside hospitals?
faq.a: Across approximately 3,500 sequenced genomes from a regional One Health study around Pavia, the researchers found no carbapenem-non-susceptible Klebsiella pneumoniae outside hospitals. Ed stresses that this does not prove absence, and that the study did not select for antibiotic resistance.

faq.q: Does finding a resistance gene mean a bacterium is resistant?
faq.a: Not necessarily. The guests describe resistance plasmids in bacteria that were not phenotypically resistant and discuss how resistance-gene expression can be silenced.
